In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

(a) good hay is made from dry material, baled when the moisture content is about 16%; (b) hay baled at about this moisture content heats little and moulds little; (c) wet bales heat to about 60°-65°C and mould with thermophilic fungi; (d) hay is not made from wet material, baled at about a 40% moisture content.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the moulding of hay is a complex process, which depends upon the moisture content of the hay at the time of baling and upon the temperature subsequently reached.
hays baled at 20 % moisture or above are liable to heat to 60° or more and mould with a thermophilic flora, which is largely absent from the dry hays.
hay baled at 25 % moisture or less is suitable for good hay, but hay baled at higher moisture contents is unsuitable for good hay, and should be stored in stacks.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the microbial and biochemical characteristics of hay are determined by the initial moisture content of the hay and the temperature subsequently attained, and that the hay type is related to the type of micro-organisms present.
the type of hay obtained is dependent on the initial moisture content and on the temperature to which it is subjected.
the quality of the hay is related to the initial water content and temperature attained.
